subsection: 8. Demographic growth and affluence: consumerism, leisure, work, women and the family

notes.h: The baby boom and population shifts
notes.b: After 1945 Americans had wartime savings and pent-up demand, and they married early and had many children. The result was a population boom and a great movement of people, both of which created huge new demand for homes and goods.
points: The baby boom ran from about 1946 to 1964, with births peaking in 1957 at about 4.3 million in a single year. It followed the end of the war, a prosperous economy and early marriage.
Families were larger than in the 1930s, and the average age of first marriage fell during the 1950s, so more young couples were setting up homes and buying goods at the same time.
Dr Benjamin Spock's The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946) sold millions of copies, which is why historians link it with how the boom generation was raised.
The suburbs, the residential rings around the edge of cities, were the fastest-growing part of the country in the 1950s, because families wanted space and could now afford new houses.
As the suburbs grew, several older northern industrial cities, such as Detroit, began losing population in the 1950s, which left the city centres with fewer of the white middle-class residents.

The Sun Belt, the South and Southwest from Florida to California, grew rapidly after 1945, helped by air conditioning, which made the hot climate liveable, and by federal defence spending, which brought jobs.
California passed New York as the most populous state in the early 1960s, a measure of how far the Sun Belt had grown.

The Great Migration, the movement of black Americans from the South to northern and western cities such as Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles, continued after 1945, while white families moved out to the suburbs in a pattern called white flight.
notes.tip: Say the suburbs were the fastest-growing area of the country in the 1950s. Do not claim that suburbs already had more people than the cities by 1960.

notes.h: Suburbia and the mass market for housing
notes.b: Mass-produced houses on new suburban estates, financed by federal mortgage guarantees, became the physical image of the American Dream (the belief that hard work brings a home, prosperity and upward mobility). They also showed that this Dream was not open to everyone.
points: Wartime savings and pent-up demand in 1945, together with federal housing help for veterans under the GI Bill (1944), meant that many families wanted to buy a home as soon as houses were available.

William Levitt's firm began Levittown on Long Island, New York, in 1947, with about 17,000 houses. They were built with specialised teams for each stage on mass-production lines, which kept costs low.
The first Levittown houses were small Cape Cod style homes sold for under 8,000 dollars, so ordinary families, not only the rich, could afford to buy.
Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Veterans Administration (VA) mortgage guarantees let buyers borrow with a small deposit or none, on long repayment terms.

Levittown leases excluded black buyers. The Supreme Court ruled restrictive covenants (clauses barring sales to certain groups) unenforceable in Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), but lending practices and private rules still kept most black families out of new suburbs.
The suburbs were built around the car, with new highways and shopping centres replacing the public transport and downtown shops of the older cities.
Television sets were in most American homes by 1960, and advertising on television promoted the goods that suburban households were expected to buy.

In the Kitchen Debate in Moscow in July 1959, Richard Nixon and Nikita Khrushchev argued in a model American house and kitchen at the American National Exhibition. Nixon claimed that suburban abundance proved the superiority of capitalism over communism.
notes.tip: The Kitchen Debate took place in a model house in Moscow, not at Levittown. For short questions on Levittown give where, when, why it was cheap (mass production and mortgage guarantees) and who was excluded.

notes.b: Consumerism is a culture in which buying goods, encouraged by advertising and credit, is central to life and identity. In the 1950s mass production, instalment buying and television turned shopping into a way of showing who you were.
points: Diners Club, launched in 1950, was an early charge card, and BankAmericard, launched in 1958, became the forerunner of Visa. Do not confuse the two: one was a charge card, the other an early credit card.
Credit let families buy cars, appliances and furniture on instalments, so spending was no longer limited to the income they had that week.
Shopping malls, supermarkets and department stores spread through the suburbs, and goods such as dishwashers, freezers and automatic washing machines became common in middle-class homes.
Television was in about 9 per cent of homes in 1950 and about 87 per cent in 1960. Advertising reached the living room, and sponsors paid for programmes such as I Love Lucy.
Advertising agencies used television, magazines and market research (studying what buyers want) to create demand for new products, and brand loyalty became a central marketing aim.
Vance Packard's The Hidden Persuaders (1957) accused advertisers of using psychological methods to manipulate buyers.
John Kenneth Galbraith's The Affluent Society (1958) argued that private affluence sat beside neglected public services, and that advertising created wants that consumers did not really need.
Disneyland opened in California in July 1955, and leisure industries such as theme parks and motels grew with the car and the family holiday.
notes.tip: Strong essays name a critic of affluence, Galbraith or Packard, and say what he argued, rather than describing affluence alone. Use dated evidence such as Levittown 1947, credit cards and television.

notes.h: Leisure and the role of work
notes.b: Rising incomes and a shorter working week gave Americans more time and money for leisure. At the same time, work in large organisations shaped how middle-class men saw themselves.
points: The standard working week was about forty hours, and paid holidays became more widespread in the 1950s and 1960s, which gave families time for trips and recreation.
Leisure centred on the home, television and the car, with the suburban backyard a key place of recreation and the car holiday a new family habit.
White-collar jobs (office, management, sales and service work) grew faster than manufacturing jobs from the 1950s onwards, so more workers were salaried employees rather than factory hands.

William H. Whyte's The Organization Man (1956) described the salaried corporate employee who values loyalty and conformity, and it criticised a culture in which large companies shaped how middle-class men lived.
The male breadwinner ideal, the belief that the husband should earn the family income, was celebrated by the suburban culture of the 1950s, which left the wife with the home.
notes.tip: The Organization Man is a book, not a person. Use it to show Whyte's picture of corporate conformity when discussing work.

notes.b: The 1950s promoted domesticity for women, but in practice more and more women, including married women, took paid jobs. Their pay and range of jobs stayed limited, and family life itself began to change.
points: Many women left wartime industrial jobs after 1945 and were pushed out. The media then promoted the domestic ideal in magazines, films and advice literature.
From the 1950s women's share of the paid workforce rose steadily, as married women with children increasingly took jobs outside the home.
Women were about 30 per cent of the labour force in 1950 and about 38 per cent in 1970, but they were concentrated in clerical, teaching, nursing and sales jobs at lower pay.
Divorce rates rose and single-parent families increased from the 1960s and 1970s. This weakened the ideal of the traditional nuclear family of a breadwinner father and a housewife mother.
Enovid, the first contraceptive pill, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration for contraception in May 1960, which gave women greater control over the timing of births.
Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) was a Supreme Court decision that struck down a ban on contraception for married couples.
notes.tip: Griswold (1965) concerned contraception for married couples, while Roe v. Wade (1973) concerned abortion. Examiners ask for the post-war return to the home, rising employment and laws with years, so give the 30 per cent and 38 per cent figures as evidence of rising employment.

notes.h: Women's rights: laws, courts and the ERA
notes.b: From the 1960s federal law and the courts began to challenge sex discrimination. Each measure dealt with a different area of life and had limits, and conservative women organised against the Equal Rights Amendment.
points: The Equal Pay Act of 10 June 1963 applied to men and women doing equal work in the same establishment. Enforcement was weak, so low pay for women continued.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned employment discrimination on grounds of sex as well as race, colour, religion and national origin. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforced it.
Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 banned sex discrimination in federally funded education. Do not confuse it with Title VII, which dealt with employment.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974 made it illegal to refuse credit to a woman on the basis of her sex or marital status. It mattered because credit was central to consumer life.
Roe v. Wade (22 January 1973) was a Supreme Court ruling that the Constitution protects a woman's decision to have an abortion, at least in the early stages of pregnancy.
The Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) passed Congress in March 1972. The ratification deadline was extended to 1982, but only 35 of the 38 states needed had ratified, so it failed.
Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign began in 1972 and mobilised conservative women who argued that the amendment threatened the family, which helped to block ratification.
notes.tip: Weak answers list laws without saying what changed. For each law say what it did and its limits, such as weak enforcement of the 1963 Act and continuing low pay and a narrow range of jobs.

notes.b: Friedan was both a witness to and a victim of the domestic ideal she attacked, and she became a central figure in second-wave feminism (the movement for women's equal rights revived in the 1960s).
points: Betty Friedan was born in Peoria, Illinois, in 1921 and studied psychology at Smith College. She wrote magazine articles while she was a housewife and mother in the suburbs, so she knew the life she described.
Her survey of her former Smith College classmates about their lives formed the basis of The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963.
The Feminine Mystique argued that American women were trapped by a domestic ideal, the feminine mystique, which denied them fulfilment. She called their condition the 'problem that has no name'.
The book sold very widely and is credited with helping to start the second wave of the American feminist movement.

In June 1966 Friedan founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) and became its first president, aiming to secure equal rights for women in employment and law. NOW pressed for the ERA, which failed to be ratified by 1982.

She organised the Women's Strike for Equality on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment (which gave women the vote), and helped to found the National Women's Political Caucus in 1971.
Contemporaries were divided. Supporters admired her as a campaigner for women's rights, conservatives attacked her, and younger radical feminists found her too moderate.
Historians judge her a central figure who helped start the second wave. They criticise The Feminine Mystique for focusing on white middle-class women, and criticise her hostility to lesbians in NOW.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the book (1963), the organisation NOW (1966) and the ERA (Congress 1972, never ratified): Friedan did not write the ERA. A list of the book alone scores low, so add what she did afterwards and how she was judged.

notes.h: Key personality: Marilyn Monroe as an image of women
notes.b: Monroe's screen image stood for 1950s ideals of glamour and desirability, and it was closely tied to consumer culture. Here she is treated only as an image of women.
points: She was born Norma Jeane Mortenson in Los Angeles in 1926 and became a model and then a film star, taking the name Marilyn Monroe.

Her films, including Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), How to Marry a Millionaire (1953) and The Seven Year Itch (1955), presented a glamorous, sexually attractive and childlike blonde, an image that was widely copied.
Her image was used in advertisements and magazines that sold products by linking them to her appeal, which tied her closely to the consumer culture of the 1950s.

Hollywood marketed her as a sex symbol and typecast her. She resisted by founding Marilyn Monroe Productions in 1955 and studying at the Actors Studio in New York, and she won acclaim for Some Like It Hot (1959).
Contemporaries admired her beauty and screen presence, but she was criticised as a sex symbol rather than a serious actress.
Later feminist critics read her image as a product of a male-dominated film industry that limited women's roles to decorative or passive parts.
Historians now treat her as a symbol of both the glamour and the constraints placed on women in the 1950s. Her image fitted the ideal of femininity that Friedan attacked.
notes.tip: In a Friedan and Monroe answer, present Monroe as the 1950s ideal of glamour and its constraints, and Friedan as the challenge to the domestic ideal, and link them through consumer culture.

notes.h: Assessment: did affluence deliver the American Dream?
notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement stated at the start and supported by paired points, which weigh the material gains of the period against the groups left out. The Dream was real for many but unevenly shared by race, class and sex.
points: Achievements: home ownership, rising incomes and the spread of consumer goods gave millions of white middle-class families a standard of living that earlier generations had not known.
Limits: lending practices and private rules excluded most black families from the suburbs, and the poor were left out of the affluence, so the Dream was unevenly shared by race and class.
Women's gains: more women, including married women, held jobs and gained new legal rights such as the 1963 Equal Pay Act and Title VII of 1964.
Women's limits: pay stayed low and the range of jobs narrow, and Friedan's evidence showed that many women felt the domestic ideal failed them.
Critics: Galbraith, Packard and Whyte questioned the quality of affluent life, arguing that it brought manufactured wants, manipulation and conformity.
Overall: by the 1970s the family and women's roles had changed, because divorce, single-parent families and women's employment had all increased.
notes.tip: For the 100-mark essay state your judgement at the start and give paired points with dated evidence such as Levittown 1947, credit cards, television and the 1974 Credit Act.

keyTerms.definition: The culture that encouraged the continual purchase of goods, promoted through advertising and credit, and which became central to American life after 1945.
The movement for equal rights for women, which revived in the 1960s and campaigned for equal pay, employment protection and access to contraception and abortion.
Betty Friedan's 1963 book arguing that American women were trapped by a domestic ideal that denied them fulfilment.
The organisation founded in June 1966 by Betty Friedan and others to campaign for equal rights for women.
The mass-produced suburban development on Long Island, New York, begun in 1947, which became a symbol of suburban life.
The southern and south-western states, from Florida to California, which grew rapidly in population and industry after 1945.
The rise in the birth rate after the Second World War, lasting from about 1946 to 1964.
The belief that hard work and opportunity would bring home ownership, prosperity and upward mobility to every family.
The movement of white families from central cities to the suburbs, which left many cities poorer and more racially segregated.
The Supreme Court decision of 22 January 1973 that held that the Constitution protected a woman's right to choose an abortion in the early stages of pregnancy.
